A long dry period that began around 2200 BCE, about 4,200 years ago, and probably lasted through most of the 22nd century BCE. It was one of the most severe climate events of the last 12,000 years, and geologists use it to mark the start of the current Meghalayan age, named after a cave in northeast India whose stalagmites record it.

It shows up in lake beds, cave deposits and ocean cores from the Mediterranean to China. Rainfall seems to have dropped across a wide belt of the Near East and South Asia, and the monsoon weakened.

It lines up in time with several collapses:

  • The Akkadian Empire in Mesopotamia fell apart, and northern Syrian towns such as Tell Leilan were abandoned.
  • Egypt's Old Kingdom ended; low Nile floods and famine are described in texts of the First Intermediate Period that followed.
  • In the Indus Valley, the great cities began a slow decline, and people moved east toward wetter land.
  • In China, the Liangzhu culture of the lower Yangtze had already ended.

How far the drought caused these events is debated. The dates of the climate records and of the collapses are not precise, the effects differed from place to place, and states also fell for political reasons. Many historians now see it as a strain that tested societies rather than a single cause of their fall.
